paragraphs.heading: Stone that grows in caves
paragraphs.text: A speleothem is a rock formation built up over time from minerals left behind in natural caves. The word joins the Ancient Greek terms for cave and deposit. Their shapes depend on how and where the minerals were laid down, and the familiar ones are stalagmites, stalactites and flowstones. More than 300 kinds of cave mineral deposit have been identified.

paragraphs.heading: What they are made of
paragraphs.text: Speleothems most often form in caves made of carbonate rock, through reactions that dissolve carbonate. Nearly all of them are calcium carbonate (CaCO₃), in the form of the minerals calcite or aragonite. A smaller number are made of calcium sulfate, as gypsum or mirabilite, or of opal.

paragraphs.heading: Colours and shapes
paragraphs.text: Pure calcium carbonate or calcium sulfate speleothems are clear and colourless. Iron oxide or copper turns them reddish brown, manganese oxide can make them black or dark brown, and mud and silt can make them brown. Many things shape them, including the chemistry of the rock and water, how fast and in what direction water seeps and flows, the cave's temperature, humidity and air currents, and the climate and plants above ground. Weak drips falling a short way build narrow stalagmites, while heavy flow and a long fall tend to build wide ones.

paragraphs.heading: A climate diary in stone
paragraphs.text: Their chemistry, slow growth and safe keeping inside caves make speleothems useful proxies, or stand-in records, of past climate. A slice across one can hold a climate record much like an ice core or a tree's rings. Because they grow slowly and take in radioactive elements, they can be dated accurately over much of the late Quaternary with radiocarbon and uranium-thorium dating. That works as long as the cave stayed a closed system and the speleothem has not recrystallized.

paragraphs.heading: How scientists read them
paragraphs.text: Stable isotopes of oxygen (δ¹⁸O) and carbon (δ¹³C) track changes in rainfall temperature, precipitation and plant cover over roughly the past 500,000 years. The rings matter too: tightly packed rings mean little rain, widely spaced rings mean heavier rain, and denser rings mean more moisture. Counting drip rates and analysing trace elements in the drops records short-term swings such as El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) events. The Mg/Ca ratio also serves as a moisture gauge, though cave ventilation in dry seasons can make it less reliable.

paragraphs.heading: Old records and odd shapes
paragraphs.text: In a rare case, climate data from the early Permian period came from speleothems 289 million years old, found in filled-in caves that quarrying opened up at Richards Spur in Oklahoma. Some speleothems ignore gravity altogether. Helictites grow when water is pressed through tiny pores in the bedrock and a cave crust, and their direction is set by surface tension or by crystal structure, not by gravity.

paragraphs.heading: Look-alikes outside caves
paragraphs.text: Similar shapes can form from concrete, lime, mortar or other carbonate material outside caves or in man-made spaces such as mines and tunnels. The usual definition leaves these out. Deposits like these in man-made structures are called calthemites, and they often go along with crumbling concrete or with lime, mortar or similar material being washed out.
